title: The missing necklace at the craft show
passage:
Last Friday, our school held a craft show. My friend Lucy lost her handmade necklace. It was made of colourful beads and was very special to her. She felt sad and asked me to be her detective partner.
First, we asked Lucy's deskmate, Lily. Lily said she didn't see the necklace. Then we thought: where did Lucy go before the show? She told us she went to the playground to get some fresh air. We went to the playground and looked carefully. Suddenly, I saw something shiny under a tree—it was Lucy's necklace! Lucy said she put the necklace in her bag before going to the playground. Lucy was so happy to get it back. She said I was a clever detective because I used good thinking skills to find the clue.

title: The thief's secret message
passage: One night, a thief stole many jewels from a big house. The next morning, a detective came to look for clues. He walked around the house and looked carefully. He found a letter under the table. The thief wrote to his wife and wanted to tell her where the jewels were, but he wrote in a secret way. The detective read the first letters of each word. They spelled a word: BRIDGE. It meant the old bridge! The police waited near the bridge. When the thief came to get the jewels, they caught him. Working out a message is like solving a puzzle. If you look carefully, you can solve many problems!

title: Using leaves to find the way
passage: One day, a little boy was walking in the forest and lost his way. He took a deep breath and did not give up. He remembered his grandfather's words: use what is around you to help. He looked at the trees. On the side with more leaves, the sun shines more, so that side is south. He also used some long leaves to mark the path behind him. Slowly, he walked out of the forest and saw his village. His mother was worried, but she was so glad to see him. The boy learned that a calm mind and careful observation can work out any problem.

title: Who took the pencil case?
passage: In our class, Xiao Ming's pencil case was missing. It had his favourite pens and a new ruler. Our teacher asked us to work it out as a class mystery. First, we checked the classroom corner by corner. Lily said she saw it on the desk after lunch. Then we asked Tom, who sat near Xiao Ming. Tom said he picked up a dropped case and put it on the bookshelf. We looked on the bookshelf and found it behind some books. Everyone clapped. We learned that when something goes missing, we should ask questions, check clues and never jump to conclusions.

title: My school, then and now
passage:
My school has changed a lot. Ten years ago, it was small. There was only one tall building and a small playground. There were no computers in the classroom. Students had to read books to learn new things. The journey to school was hard for some students; they had to walk a long way.
Now my school is big and beautiful. There are three tall buildings and a big playground with a football field. Every classroom has many computers. Students can use the internet to learn more. All the students can take the school bus to school, so the journey is easy and safe. We all love our new school.

title: Planting hope on the bare mountain
passage: Twenty years ago, the mountain near the village was bare. There were almost no trees, and the wind blew dust everywhere. Uncle Li and the villagers decided to change it. They started to plant trees on the mountain year after year. At first, many young trees died, but they did not give up. Today, there are millions of trees on the mountain. The weather is nice, and it is not windy and dusty any more. The mountain is green and the village is beautiful. When Uncle Li says "we planted hope", he means the mountain became green and the village got beautiful. Trees bring a better life to everyone.

title: Mike's town, thirty years ago and now
passage:
Mike lives in a small town in the south of China. Thirty years ago, his town was very small. There were only a few small houses and narrow roads. There was no teahouse, no supermarket and no internet at home. People mainly travelled by bike or on foot.
Now the town is different. There are many tall buildings and shops. A beautiful teahouse stands by the river. Shared bikes are everywhere, and people can also travel by high-speed train. People have the internet at home and life is much easier. Mike says his town changes fast, but it keeps its warm heart.

title: Changes bring a better life
passage:
Thirty years ago, life in China was very different. People lived in small houses and there were not many cars. The streets were full of bikes, and most people went to work by bike. In the past, the journey to school was hard and dangerous; some children walked for hours over mountains.
Today, everything is different. There are lots of tall buildings and wide roads. People leave home in the morning and get to another city by high-speed train in hours. Grandpa told me some young people gave up a good life in the city to do something for their hometown. After 22 years, the Daliang Mountains became a green world with over 10 million trees. Changes bring us a better life, and we should love our country.

title: The Golden Touch（教材Speed up）
passage:
Long long ago, there was a king called Midas. He loved gold very much. One day he met an old man. The old man said, "Do you have a wish? I can make it come true."
"I wish for a golden touch," said Midas. "I want to turn everything to gold!" "Are you sure?" "Yes. I am very sure."
Midas turned everything around him to gold. He was happy. Then Midas was hungry, but all his food also turned to gold. His daughter came in. Midas took her hand. She turned to gold, too! Midas was very sad. He cried, "I don't want gold now. I want food. I want my daughter back." He asked the old man to get everything back again. When he asked how much it would cost, the old man did not ask for gold; he only wanted Midas to learn the lesson. The old man smiled, "Just remember, gold isn't everything." When we save a little each time, the coins slowly grow into something useful. Sharing a small amount with people in need brings more joy than keeping it all. From now on, wise children write down what they spend and plan what they save. Money is not just coins in a pocket; it is a choice we make every week. After reading it, we may think of our own experiences and find a similar moment in ourselves. The more we read, the more we connect these ideas with the people and events around us. Talking about it with classmates helps us understand the passage from different points of view. Looking back, the story teaches us a small but useful lesson that we can carry into our daily school life.
passageZh:
很久很久以前，有一位名叫迈达斯的国王，他非常热爱黄金。一天他遇见一位老人，老人说：“你有愿望吗？我能让它实现。”
“我希望有点石成金的本领，”迈达斯说，“我要把一切都变成黄金！”“你确定吗？”“是的，我非常确定。”
迈达斯把身边的一切都变成了黄金，他很开心。后来他饿了，可所有食物也变成了黄金。女儿走进来，迈达拉住她的手，她也变成了黄金！迈达斯非常伤心，哭着说：“我现在不要黄金了，我要食物，我要女儿回来。”他请老人把一切变回来。当他问要付出多少代价时，老人没有要黄金，只想让迈达斯吸取教训。老人笑着说：“记住，黄金不是万能的。” 每次存下一点，硬币就会慢慢攒成有用的数目。把一小部分分给需要帮助的人，比独自占有带来更多快乐。从现在起，聪明的孩子会记下自己的开销，并规划要存下的钱。钱不只是口袋里的硬币，它是我们每周都要做的一种选择。读完它，我们会联想到自己的经历，在自己身上找到相似的一刻。读得越多，我们越能把这些道理和身边的人与事联系起来。和同学讨论它，能让我们从不同角度理解这篇短文。回头看，这个故事带给我们一个细小却有用的道理，可以带进日常的校园生活。
source: 外研版（新标准·三起）；六上教材PDF Speed up《The Golden Touch》（真实故事，Unit 1）

title: Tom's Pocket Money
passage: Tom received fifty yuan every month as pocket money. At the shop, he always bought toys or sweets. He never saved a coin. One day, he saw a notice on the school board. It said that some children in the mountains had no new pencils or books. Tom felt a little sad, but he did not know what to do. His mother advised him to keep a money diary. She said, "Write down every yuan you spend. Then you will see where your money goes." Tom tried for one week. He found that he spent twenty yuan on crisps and chocolate. He was surprised. The next month, he decided to save half of his money. He put the coins in a piggy bank. After three months, he had seventy-five yuan. He sent the money to the children in the mountains with a short letter. A week later, he received a thank-you drawing from a girl there. Tom put the drawing on his wall. title: Lily's Opinion About Breakfast
passage: In my opinion, breakfast is the most important meal of the day. Some of my classmates skip breakfast because they get up late. They say they are not hungry in the morning. But I don't think so. I feel tired if I do not eat breakfast, and I cannot listen carefully in class. Last week, our science teacher did a small test. We compared two groups. Group One ate eggs, bread and milk for breakfast. Group Two ate only a sweet cake. After two hours, Group One was much more active. The children who ate sweet food became sleepy very early. Our teacher explained: sweet food gives a quick but short energy, while milk and eggs give a longer and steadier energy. In my opinion, a good breakfast should include milk, eggs or bread, and some fruit. It is better to get up ten minutes earlier than to skip breakfast. title: Xu Xiake, the Great Traveller
passage: Xu Xiake is one of the most famous travellers in Chinese history. He was born in 1587, in the Ming Dynasty. When he was a boy, he loved reading books about mountains and rivers. His dream was to see them with his own eyes. At that time, most people stayed close to home. But Xu Xiake wanted to explore the world. For more than thirty years, he travelled on foot and on horseback. He climbed dangerous mountains, crossed deep rivers and walked through thick forests. He did not travel for fun only. Every day, he wrote in his diary. He described rocks, rivers, plants and the homes of local people. His notes later became a great book called The Travel Diaries of Xu Xiake. Modern scientists are surprised by his records. They say his descriptions of caves and rivers are surprisingly accurate. Reading a travel book is a good way to know a place before we visit it ourselves. Protecting a forest means protecting its birds, rivers, soil and quiet air as well. Nature shows us the highest mountain, the longest river and the deepest lake of the world. These wonders belong to everyone, so we should leave them clean for the next generation. title: A Trip to the National Park
passage: Last summer, our class went to Zhangjiajie National Park. We went there by bus early in the morning. When we arrived, we saw tall, strange mountains rising straight into the clouds. Our teacher said these mountains were made of stone, and the wind and rain had shaped them over millions of years. We took a small train through a deep valley. The trees were so thick that the sun could hardly reach the ground. We saw colourful birds and heard monkeys jumping in the trees. At noon, we had a picnic near a clear river. The water was so cold that our fingers turned red. In the afternoon, we walked along a glass bridge high above the valley. Some of us were afraid to look down, but the view was amazing. Our teacher told us not to drop litter. She said, "These rocks and trees have lived for millions of years. We are only visitors. We must leave them as we found them." On the way home, everyone was tired, but no one stopped talking about the trip. We all agreed that protecting nature is everyone's duty. Protecting a forest means protecting its birds, rivers, soil and quiet air as well. Nature shows us the highest mountain, the longest river and the deepest lake of the world. These wonders belong to everyone, so we should leave them clean for the next generation. Reading a travel book is a good way to know a place before we visit it ourselves. title: The Amazon Rainforest
passage: The Amazon rainforest is the largest forest on the earth. It covers most of Brazil and eight other countries. People call it the "lungs of the earth", because it produces a huge amount of oxygen. Millions of kinds of animals and plants live there. Some of them have not even been discovered by scientists. The forest is always wet and warm. Tall trees block the sunlight, so the ground below is dark and quiet. However, this amazing forest is getting smaller every year. People cut down trees to make farms, roads and shopping centres. When the trees disappear, many animals lose their homes. The climate also changes, because the forest can no longer hold so much water. Experts say that if we lose the Amazon, the whole planet will feel the effect. Some groups are working hard to stop the cutting. They plant new trees and teach local people how to live without destroying the forest. In my opinion, protecting the rainforest is not just one country's business. It is a duty for everyone on the earth. The next generation should be able to walk into a living forest, not a dead one. title: The Longest River Quiz
passage: Last Monday, our teacher held a "Wonders of Nature" quiz. There were five groups, and our group hoped to win. The first question was: "What is the longest river in the world?" Daming quickly said, "The Nile!" The teacher nodded and gave us ten points. The next question was: "Which is the highest mountain?" We answered Mount Qomolangma. Then came a hard one: "Which is the deepest lake in the world?" We thought for a minute. Lingling said, "Baikal!" It was correct. The last question was a surprise: "Who wrote about Chinese mountains and rivers more than three hundred years ago?" We looked at each other. Suddenly, Sam shouted, "Xu Xiake!" We won the quiz by two points. After that, the teacher showed us photos of different wonders. She said, "There are so many wonders on the earth, but we must protect them." We decided to make a poster about nature protection for our school. The quiz was not only about remembering facts. It made us love and care for our beautiful planet. These wonders belong to everyone, so we should leave them clean for the next generation. Reading a travel book is a good way to know a place before we visit it ourselves. title: Lu Ban and the Umbrella（教材Speed up）
passage:
It was raining. Grandpa gave Lingling an umbrella. "Grandpa, who first got the idea of making an umbrella?" she asked.
Grandpa said no one knows for sure, but stories say it was Lu Ban. One day, Lu Ban was on the way home and it rained. He thought, "What can I make to keep off the rain?" Just then, he saw a boy with a big leaf over his head. "That's a good idea!" Lu Ban said.
First, he used bamboo to make the sticks. Next, he cut some cloth. Then, he put the cloth over the sticks. That was the first umbrella! Lu Ban had great ideas and clever hands. title: The Recycling Club
passage: Our school started a Recycling Club this term. Every Wednesday afternoon, members meet in the art room. title: A Dress from an Old Scarf
passage: Last winter, Anna's mother gave her a beautiful dress. It was not new from a shop. Her mother made it from an old wool scarf. The scarf was Anna's grandmother's. The dress was soft and blue, with two buttons on the front. Anna loved it very much. At school, her friend Julia asked where she bought it. Anna smiled and said, "My mum made it from Grandma's old scarf." Julia was surprised. She said, "I have an old sweater at home with a hole. Can your mum help me?" Anna's mother agreed. Soon, she helped several girls turn old clothes into new bags and scarves. The children learnt that old cloth does not have to be rubbish. It can become something full of love. title: Reduce, Reuse, Recycle
passage: You may have heard the three words: Reduce, Reuse, Recycle. They are the rules for a greener life. "Reduce" means use less. For example, take your own bag to the shop, so you do not need a new plastic one. Turn off the light when you leave a room. "Reuse" means use things again. Don't throw away a glass jar. You can keep pencils or sweets in it. Give old books to a library instead of putting them in the bin. "Recycle" means change waste into new materials. Paper, glass, cans and plastic can be processed and made into new products. Many families in our street now sort their rubbish into four boxes: paper, plastic, glass and kitchen waste. Kitchen waste can become natural fertilizer for plants. Our class did a survey. We found that each student threw away about three plastic bottles a week. That is over one hundred bottles a year, for one child alone. If everyone reduces a little, the numbers will drop. We do not need great heroes. We need millions of people who do small things right. title: Ten Rules for a Healthy Life
passage: Do you want to be healthy and strong? Here are ten simple rules from a school doctor. First, drink enough water every day, about six glasses. Second, sleep for at least eight hours. Ninth, be kind to others. Helping friends brings you happiness, and happiness is good for your body. Tenth, remember that health is more important than marks or games. title: The Boy Who Hated Carrots

title: A Good Night's Sleep
passage: Sleep is like a silent doctor. While we sleep, our body repairs itself. Our brain organises what we learned during the day. However, many children do not sleep enough. A survey in our city showed that about sixty percent of Grade Six students slept less than eight hours. The main reason was screens. Many children played on their phones or watched videos until after ten o'clock. A doctor said that too much screen light makes the brain think it is still daytime. As a result, children feel tired the next day. They cannot listen carefully, and they may even feel ill. The doctor gave some advice. First, stop using screens one hour before bed. Second, keep the bedroom dark and quiet. Third, go to bed at the same time every night. Fourth, do not drink sweet drinks in the evening. After reading the survey, our class made a "Sleep Pact". We agreed to turn off our phones at nine thirty. After two weeks, most of us said we felt more awake in class. A good night's sleep costs nothing, but it gives us everything. Good habits, such as early sleep and daily exercise, protect us from many illnesses. When we are sick, rest and medicine help, but prevention is always the best way. title: Chinese Tea Culture
passage: China is the home of tea. Chinese people have drunk tea for thousands of years. Every region has its own famous tea. Longjing comes from Hangzhou, and Pu'er comes from Yunnan. When a guest visits a Chinese home, the host will often serve a cup of tea. The guest holds the cup with both hands as a sign of respect. My foreign friend, Anna, learnt this last month. She visited her classmate Xiao Ming's home for dinner. Mrs Wang, Xiao Ming's mum, brought out a small pot of green tea. "How fresh the smell is!" Anna said. Mrs Wang smiled and said, "In China, tea is not just a drink. It is a way to welcome friends." Anna watched carefully. She saw that the tea cup was small, and the tea was poured only half full. She asked why. Xiao Ming explained that in Chinese culture, a full cup means you want the guest to leave. Half a cup means care and friendship. Anna was surprised by these small but meaningful rules. She said, "How interesting your culture is!" Mrs Wang agreed: China is a beautiful and interesting place, and every custom has a story behind it. title: The Lantern Festival
passage: The Lantern Festival is on the fifteenth day of the first lunar month. It is the end of the Spring Festival celebrations. On that night, towns and parks are filled with colourful lanterns. What a beautiful sight it is! There are lanterns of all shapes: rabbits, dragons, fish and even cartoon characters. People write riddles on small pieces of paper and tie them to the lanterns. Visitors guess the riddles, and the right answers win small gifts. Food is an important part of the festival. People eat sweet rice balls called tangyuan. The round shape means family togetherness. Last year, our family went to the lantern show in the old town. My little sister ran from one lantern to another, pointing and laughing. How excited she was! My father took many photos. My mother bought a lantern shaped like a rabbit. We ate hot tangyuan while walking in the cold air. How warm the food felt inside! Many people say the Spring Festival is not truly over until the Lantern Festival ends. We love this festival, because it brings the whole family together under a sky of light. title: Meet the Panda Keeper
passage: Last Friday, our class visited the Chengdu Panda Base. We were lucky to meet Miss Zhou, a panda keeper. She has worked there for ten years. "What does a panda keeper do?" Daming asked. Miss Zhou smiled. She said, "We clean the enclosures, prepare fresh bamboo, and watch the pandas' health." She showed us a basket of fresh bamboo. "How much bamboo does a panda eat a day?" Lingling asked. "About twelve to thirty-eight kilograms," Miss Zhou answered. We were all surprised. Miss Zhou told us that pandas spend most of their day eating and sleeping. She also told us not to make loud noises or get too close. Pandas are shy animals. At noon, we watched a baby panda climb onto a wooden frame and then roll down. How cute it was! We all laughed. Miss Zhou said pandas are national treasures. Protecting them is a big job. She invited us to learn more about wildlife. Before leaving, we took a group photo with Miss Zhou. title: A Foreign Student in Beijing
passage: Peter is a fourteen-year-old boy from Canada. Last year, he came to Beijing as an exchange student. At first, everything was new and difficult. He could not read the Chinese menus, and he did not know how to take the subway. But his host family, the Chens, were very kind. Mrs Chen taught him to use chopsticks. Mr Chen took him to the Great Wall on a cool Saturday. "What a long wall it is!" Peter said, looking down from the watchtower. In Beijing, Peter tried many new things. He ate jianbing for breakfast, watched Beijing opera, and even learnt a few Chinese songs. He found that Chinese people were warm and helpful. When he got lost, a grandfather helped him find the right bus. Peter said, "How lucky I am to experience this culture!" At the end of the year, he could speak simple Chinese. He made many Chinese friends. Peter learned an important lesson: when you visit a new country, respect its customs, and the people will welcome you. When in Rome, do as the Romans do. Next year, Peter wants to bring his whole family to China. When we visit a new place, a polite smile and kind words are understood everywhere. title: At the Fast-food Restaurant
passage: Last Saturday, the children went to a fast-food restaurant near their school. Daming opened the door and said, "I am so hungry! Can I have a hamburger?" Lingling looked at the menu. "I want a hot dog, please," she said to the waiter. Amy wanted something healthy. "I'd like a vegetable salad and a glass of water," she said. Sam could not decide. The waiter smiled and asked, "What would you like, young man?" Sam thought for a moment. "I want a chicken burger and a cola," he said. The waiter wrote everything down carefully. Then Daming asked, "How much is it all together?" The waiter added the prices: the hamburger was four dollars, the hot dog three dollars, the salad five dollars, the chicken burger four dollars, and the colas were two dollars each. Daming took out his money. "It is twenty dollars in all," he said. They found a table near the window. The food came quickly. Daming took a big bite and smiled. title: The Waiter's Mistake
passage: One day, Mr and Mrs Green took their children to a new restaurant. The waiter came to their table with a big smile. "Good evening! What would you like?" he asked. Mr Green said, "I want a steak, please." Mrs Green said, "I'd like fish and chips." Their son Tom wanted a hamburger, and their daughter Lily wanted a bowl of noodles. The waiter repeated the order and went to the kitchen. Half an hour later, the food came. But something was wrong. Mr Green was given noodles instead of steak. Mrs Green got a hamburger, not fish. Tom found fish and chips in front of him, and Lily had a steak. The children looked at each other and started to laugh. Mr Green called the waiter politely. "Excuse me," he said, "but I think there is a small mistake." The waiter's face turned red. He checked the order again and said sorry many times. He took the food back and brought the correct dishes in ten minutes. To say sorry, he gave the family a free apple pie. It was delicious. The Greens left happily. title: Eating in an English Home
passage: Last winter, Daming stayed with an English family, the Smiths. On his first evening, Mrs Smith asked, "What would you like for dinner?" Daming did not know many English food words. He said, "I want rice, please." Mr Smith smiled. "We do not eat rice every day," he said. "Tonight, we will try fish and chips." When the food came, Daming saw white fish, golden chips and a bowl of peas. Mrs Smith asked, "How much salt would you like?" Daming was surprised. In China, the cook adds salt. In England, people put salt and vinegar on their own food. Daming tried a little vinegar on his chips. It tasted different, but not bad. For dessert, Mrs Smith made apple pie. "How much is a piece?" Daming asked by habit. The whole family laughed. "At home, we do not pay for dinner," Mrs Smith said. "It is free for you." Daming felt warm. He learnt that eating in a foreign home is not just about food. It is about sharing and kindness. Before he left, he wrote a thank-you card. On it, he drew a small panda. title: The Big Mistake in the Kitchen

passageZh: 六年级后的夏天是一段重要时光。它不只是一个假期。它是连接小学和中学的桥梁。许多学生利用暑假做准备。大明买了新笔、一个书包和一本数学习题册。他还读了两本科学书。玲玲参观了新学校附近的市图书馆。她想认认路，这样第一天就不会迷路。萨姆每天早上练足球，因为他想进校队。艾米读中文故事，保持语言能力。有些学生对新学校感到担心。他们担心功课更难、新老师和交朋友。但父母告诉他们，起初每个人都会有同样的感觉。关键是要勇敢，需要时就求助。九月，他们将带着新书和大大的希望，走进校门。中学不是终点。它是一个新的开始。不同的学校，不同的梦想，但同样光明的未来，等待着每一个学生。 我们将学习语文、数学、科学以及自己选择的学科。今天说再见，并不意味着永远失去联系。写邮件、假期相聚，让旧日友谊一直延续。不同的学校带来新老师、新书、新学科和新朋友。读完它，我们会联想到自己的经历，在自己身上找到相似的一刻。读得越多，我们越能把这些道理和身边的人与事联系起来。和同学讨论它，能让我们从不同角度理解这篇短文。回头看，这个故事带给我们一个细小却有用的道理，可以带进日常的校园生活。
